title: Yelp
prompt: Design a location-based business review and discovery service like Yelp. Users search for nearby businesses by location, view reviews and ratings, and leave reviews. Target ~500M DAU globally with ~200M businesses indexed, and peak read traffic of 100k QPS from mobile location searches.

stages.title: Functional Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core functional requirements?
stages.howToAnswer: Focus on search, browse, and review. List user actions: search nearby, view details, post review. Don't drift into messaging, ads, or account management.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Spotify):
bullets: Users can search for songs by location / genre
Users can view song details and play
Users can like or playlist a song

must: Users can search for nearby businesses given a location (lat/long or address)
Users can view business details (photos, hours, ratings, reviews)
Users can submit a review with rating and text
should: Search by business name / category across the map

stages.sampleAnswer:
1. Users can search for businesses within a radius of a given location.
2. Users can view business details, reviews, and ratings.
3. Users can submit a review with a rating (1–5 stars) and optional text.
4. Users can filter by category (restaurants, bars, coffee shops, etc.).
hints: A location-based search app has a different entry point than web search. How does a user specify 'where am I looking?'
Once you find businesses, what details does the user see on the list view vs detail view?
Reviews are user-generated content. What does submitting a review require?

stages.title: Non-Functional Requirements
stages.howToAnswer: Highlight read-heavy + geospatial. Latency for nearby search, scale (DAU, businesses, QPS), availability for mobile, freshness of reviews.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Spotify):
bullets: Search results must return in <100ms p99
System should handle 100k concurrent search queries

must: Nearby search latency <200ms p99 (mobile users expect fast)
Read-heavy workload (100:1 read:write)
Scale: 200M indexed businesses, 500M DAU
Geospatial index capable of range queries (nearby within radius)
should: Availability prioritized (eventual consistency on reviews OK)
avoid: Requiring strong consistency on review visibility
Treating geospatial search as a plain keyword search

stages.sampleAnswer:
- Nearby search: <200ms p99 latency from location input to list of 20 results.
- Read:write ratio ~100:1 (searches vs reviews submitted).
- Scale: 200M businesses, 500M DAU, 100k peak QPS on search.
- Geospatial range query: find all businesses within N km of a point.
- Availability: 99.9% SLA. Eventual consistency on reviews (visible within 5s).
- Durability: a review or rating change must be persisted.
hints: Geospatial queries are fundamentally different from keyword search. What's the access pattern — distance-based or grid-based?
Mobile search is latency-sensitive. What's a reasonable p99 target for 'show me restaurants near me'?
Reviews are append-heavy but reads dominate. Does a new review need to show instantly, or is eventual consistency OK?

stages.title: Core Entities
stages.howToAnswer: List the nouns: Business, Review, User (if in scope), possibly a geospatial index proxy entity.

must: Business (name, category, location, contact, hours, rating aggregate)
should: User (optional, but needed if account scope)
avoid: Over-modeling before you know the schema

stages.sampleAnswer:
- Business: id, name, category, lat, lng, address, phone, hours, aggregateRating, reviewCount.
- Review: id, businessId, userId, rating (1–5), text, createdAt.
- Photo: id, businessId, userId, url (optional if in scope).
- User: id, name (if auth in scope).
hints: Which entity is the 'root' that geospatial queries work on?
Ratings get aggregated. Is the aggregateRating stored denormalized on the Business, or computed on read?

stages.title: API
stages.howToAnswer: One endpoint per functional requirement: search, get details, post review. REST. Include parameters for location, radius, category.

must: GET /businesses/search?lat=X&lng=Y&radius=1000 → Business[]
GET /businesses/:id → Business details with reviews
POST /reviews body: { businessId, rating, text } → 201 Review
avoid: Putting lat/lng in the path instead of query
Returning all reviews in detail endpoint (paginate)

hints: Search endpoint is the hot path. Include lat/lng as query parameters, not path. What other filtering helps the user narrow down?
The detail view can fetch reviews separately (paginated) rather than embedding all of them.
POST /reviews can be idempotent if you include a client-generated key.

stages.title: High-Level Design
stages.questionPrompt: Sketch the architecture. Walk through the search path and the review submission path.
stages.howToAnswer: Geospatial index is the headline trick. Show: client → LB → API → cache → geospatial DB (or separate index). Show review write path going to a queue/log for async indexing.

must: Geospatial index (geohash, quadtree, or S2) for nearby search
Separation of read path (search) and write path (reviews)
Aggregated rating stored denormalized or computed on read
should: Separate database or index for geospatial queries
avoid: Full-table scans to find nearby businesses (no geospatial index)
Synchronous re-aggregation of ratings on every review write

stages.sampleAnswer:
Client → ALB → API Service (stateless) → Cache (Redis) → Geospatial Index Service

Search path:
1. Client sends (lat, lng, radius, category).
2. API checks cache for recent queries in that region.
3. Cache miss → geospatial index (e.g., Elasticsearch with geo_shape, or a custom service using geohash/S2).
4. Index returns business IDs + metadata.
5. Cache populates for 5 min.
6. Response includes id, name, distance, rating.

Detail view:
1. GET /businesses/:id → fetch full details from Business DB.
2. Reviews queried separately (paginated) from Reviews DB.
3. AggregateRating recomputed on read from recent reviews, or cached if fresh enough.

Review write path:
1. POST /reviews → enqueue into a Kafka topic.
2. Review service consumes, writes to Reviews DB.
3. Async job updates aggregateRating and invalidates cache for the business.
4. Geospatial index updated eventually.

Geospatial index choice: Geohash (simple, fixed grid) or S2 (Google's library, better coverage). Geohash example: divide world into cells; for each business, compute geohash at precision 8 (110m accuracy). On search, compute geohash for user location, query nearby cells. Filter results by haversine distance to refine.
hints: The headline trick is how you find businesses within a radius without scanning all 200M. What data structure makes that fast?
Search is read-heavy (100k QPS); reviews are write-heavy but lower volume. Can they share a database, or do they need separate paths?
Geohash is one option (simple, fixed cells). S2 is another (hierarchical). Quadtree is another (tree-based). Pick one and explain why it fits.

deepDives.title: Scale to 100k QPS searches
deepDives.questionPrompt: How can your system scale to support 100k nearby searches per second?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Geospatial index is sharded by geohash prefix (or S2 cell hierarchy). Each shard is a separate index replica serving one region of the world, holding ~10–50M businesses. ALB routes by lat/lng to the appropriate shard. Within each shard, 5 read replicas (Elasticsearch nodes or custom service) share load; each handles ~4k QPS. Cache (Redis cluster, 10 shards) holds hot cells (cities, airports) with 95% hit rate, so only ~5k QPS hit the index layer. For cold regions (sparse data), the index returns directly without cache.

must: Geospatial partitioning (shard by region or geohash prefix)
Read replica count with concrete QPS per replica
Cache hit rate assumption
should: Horizontal scaling of stateless API tier
avoid: 'Just add more servers' with no layer

hints: A single geospatial index handling 100k QPS is expensive. Can you shard the index? What's the partition key?
Not all cities get the same traffic. Hot cities (SF, NYC) spike higher. How do you handle hot cells?
What's a reasonable cache hit rate for location searches? Think about user behavior.

deepDives.title: Fresh ratings & eventual consistency
deepDives.questionPrompt: A user submits a review. When does the aggregated rating on the business update? Can another user see a stale rating?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Primary path: user submits review → enqueued to Kafka. Worker processes asynchronously, writes to Reviews DB, updates Business.aggregateRating and Business.reviewCount. Recency: indexing lag is <5 seconds on average (worker processes every 100ms). Clients cache aggregateRating from detail-view fetches for 1 min, so stale reads are ≤1 min old — acceptable for eventual consistency. For critical-path latency, the search list view shows aggregateRating from cache (refreshed every 5 min from the DB). A user who just posted a review can be shown 'your review posted' (latency-free) separately from the updated aggregate (which may lag by a few seconds).

must: Async review indexing (not synchronous on write)
Concrete lag number (seconds to minutes)
Plan for stale reads
should: Separate the 'review posted' confirmation from rating aggregate update
avoid: Blocking on rating aggregation on write (breaks 100k QPS)
Claiming strong consistency for a highly-contended rating

hints: Aggregating a rating on every review write would be slow. What's the alternative?
Is it OK for a user to post a review and not see their own review in the aggregate immediately?
How do you invalidate the cached rating when it updates?

deepDives.title: Geospatial index choice
deepDives.questionPrompt: Compare geohash, quadtree, and S2 for indexing 200M businesses. Which would you pick, and why?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Geohash: simple, fixed-size grid cells. Precision 8 → ~110m cells. Look up cells in range of the user (9 cells for 111m radius). Pro: easy to implement, cacheable by cell. Con: hot-spot cells (Times Square) can have millions of businesses, range queries span many cells. Quadtree: dynamic subdivision based on density. Adapts to clumps (cities vs deserts). Pro: fewer regions to scan. Con: complex rebalancing, non-uniform cell sizes. S2: Google's hierarchical geometry library. Cells at different levels cover different areas. Pro: elegant, space-filling curve. Con: library dependency, steeper learning curve. Pick: geohash for simplicity (most engineers know it, easy to test). Use geohash at precision 8 (110m) for initial lookup, then haversine-distance filter top-20 results. If hot-spot cells become a bottleneck (millions of businesses per cell), move to S2 or add secondary index (e.g., business category + quadtree).

must: Name the three approaches
Tradeoff analysis: lookup latency vs implementation complexity
Pick one with justification
should: Mention secondary indexes for high-density areas
avoid: Vague 'geohash is better' without explaining why
Ignoring hot-spot clusters in dense cities

hints: Geohash divides the world into a fixed grid. What's a weakness in areas with millions of nearby businesses?
Quadtree is dynamic — it subdivides until each cell has ~k businesses. Why doesn't it solve the problem perfectly?
S2 is Google's answer, but does every company use it? What's the cost of rolling your own geohash index?
